headline: Boston sues over $20M grant for Roxbury street upgrades
dek: The city says the U.S. Department of Transportation unlawfully withdrew a 2022 award for safety, transit and accessibility work on three major corridors.
body: The City of Boston has gone to federal court to recover a $20 million transportation grant that officials say was withdrawn after the project included a small electric-vehicle charging component. The lawsuit, filed Sept. 28 in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts, asks the court to reverse the U.S. Department of Transportation's cancellation of the 2022 award for the Roxbury Resilient Corridors project. The filing and case number, City of Boston v. Duffy, are listed in the public docket record (https://dockets.justia.com/docket/massachusetts/madce/1:2026cv14419/306825).

The dispute centers on three Roxbury streets: Melnea Cass Boulevard, Malcolm X Boulevard and Warren Street. Boston's project page says the grant was intended to support street repairs, safer crossings, transit improvements, accessibility work, traffic-flow changes, trees, lighting, public spaces and stormwater features. The city describes the corridors as central roadways in a historically disinvested neighborhood and says the project was being developed with local residents and community organizations (https://www.boston.gov/departments/transportation/project/roxbury-resilient-corridors).

According to a Sept. 28 announcement from U.S. Rep. Ayanna Pressley and Mayor Michelle Wu, the city argues that DOT cited the project's electric-vehicle charging infrastructure as the reason for canceling the entire award. The announcement says that charging work represented less than 1% of project costs and that federal transportation officials had previously encouraged the city to include it. Those are the city's allegations about the cancellation; the lawsuit has not produced a merits ruling (https://pressley.house.gov/2026/09/28/pressley-wu-announce-lawsuit-against-trump-administration-to-protect-20-million-federal-grant-for-roxburys-street-improvements/).

The Guardian independently reported that the case names Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and was filed against the department over its decision to withdraw the money. The newspaper also reported the city's position that federal agencies cannot rewrite a program established by Congress to match changing political priorities. The department's response was not included in the sources reviewed for this report, so the federal government's legal defense and any timetable for responding remain unclear (https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/28/boston-sues-trump-administration).

The stakes are practical for people who use Roxbury's busiest routes. Boston says the project is meant to improve bus service, walking, bicycling and driving conditions at the same time. On its Warren Street project page, the city says more than 20,250 MBTA riders use that corridor each weekday and that delays can add as much as 20 minutes to an average rider's day. That page predates the lawsuit and describes the broader transit problem rather than measuring the effect of the canceled grant, but it helps explain why the city treats the award as more than a budget line (https://content.boston.gov/departments/transportation/project/warren-street-bus-priority-corridor).

Roxbury's transportation history also shapes the argument. Boston says the wide, vehicle-oriented corridors were created through eminent-domain and block-clearance decisions during the urban-renewal era of the 1960s. The city's current plan calls for safer crossings, more comfortable bus stops, shade and cooling spaces, bike infrastructure and green stormwater measures, while also trying to prevent displacement and support small businesses. Those goals remain proposed project features, not completed improvements.

The case arrives after the city had already approved accepting the federal award. A Boston City Council record from April 2025 describes the $20 million RAISE grant as funding to reconstruct and upgrade the three Roxbury corridors. The city now says the cancellation removed a major share of the money needed to move the work forward. Whether the court restores the award, sends the decision back to DOT for reconsideration or leaves the cancellation in place will determine what Boston can realistically build and when (https://content.boston.gov/departments/city-council/city-council-roll-call-votes?page=39).

For now, the lawsuit is an opening filing, not a ruling that Boston has won or that DOT acted unlawfully. The public docket shows the case was assigned to U.S. District Judge Richard G. Stearns after an initial judge recused himself on the filing date. The next meaningful developments will be the federal defendants' response, any request for interim relief and the court's decision on how the Administrative Procedure Act claims proceed. Until then, the three-corridor project remains listed by Boston as pending, with its completion year undetermined.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Boston sues over $20M Roxbury street grant
seoDescription: Boston is asking a federal court to restore a $20 million grant for safety, transit and accessibility upgrades on three Roxbury corridors.
